chemistry-killer-08.material: A 20 % (by mass) aqueous sodium hydroxide solution ($\mathrm{NaOH}$, formula mass 40) has a density of 1.2 g/mL. It is diluted with water to prepare 600 mL of 0.5 M NaOH(aq). What volume (mL) of the 20 % NaOH solution is needed? (Atomic masses H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23. Molarity $M = \frac{10xd}{M_w}$, where x is the mass percent and d is the solution density in g/mL.)
chemistry-killer-08.s.s1.prompt: A 20 % (by mass) aqueous sodium hydroxide solution ($\mathrm{NaOH}$, formula mass 40) has a density of 1.2 g/mL. It is diluted with water to prepare 600 mL of 0.5 M NaOH(aq). What volume (mL) of the 20 % NaOH solution is needed? (Atomic masses H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23. Molarity $M = \frac{10xd}{M_w}$, where x is the mass percent and d is the solution density in g/mL.)
chemistry-killer-08.s.s1.explain:
Step 1: Molarity of 20 % NaOH: $M = \frac{10 \times 20 \times 1.2}{40} = 6.0$ mol/L (1 L = 1200 g of solution containing 240 g NaOH = 6 mol).
Step 2: Solute in the target solution = 0.5 mol/L x 0.600 L = 0.30 mol (12 g NaOH).
Step 3: Moles of solute are unchanged on dilution: 6.0 x V = 0.30, V = 0.050 L = 50 mL. (Check: 12 g / 0.20 = 60 g of solution, 60 g / 1.2 g/mL = 50 mL.)
Answer: 50 mL (d). (Wrong options: 60 mL ignores density, giving M = 5.0; 72 mL multiplies 60 g by the density; 5.0 mL is a decimal-place error.)
